expectedText:
FINANCIAL POWER OF ATTORNEY
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Lee

APPOINTMENT OF AGENT
Jordan Alex Lee appoints Morgan Lee as agent (attorney-in-fact) to act on Jordan Alex Lee's behalf as described in this document. If Morgan Lee is unable or unwilling to serve, or stops serving, Jordan Alex Lee appoints Casey Lee as successor agent.

HOW A POWER OF ATTORNEY MUST BE SIGNED
California law treats a power of attorney as legally sufficient only if it contains the date of its execution, is signed by the principal (or by another adult in the principal's presence and at the principal's direction), and is either acknowledged before a notary public or signed by at least two qualifying witnesses. A witness must be an adult and must witness either the principal's signing of the document or the principal's acknowledgment of the signature; Morgan Lee may not serve as a witness to Jordan Alex Lee's power of attorney.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A power of attorney is legally sufficient if all of the following requirements are satisfied: (a) The power of attorney contains the date of its execution. (b) The power of attorney is signed either (1) by the principal or (2) in the principal's name by another adult in the principal's presence and at the principal's direction. (c) The power of attorney is either (1) acknowledged before a notary public or (2) signed by at least two witnesses who satisfy the requirements of Section 4122."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4121 (California Legislative Information text), legal sufficiency requirements: date, signature, notarization or two witnesses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4121)
  "If the power of attorney is signed by witnesses, as provided in Section 4121, the following requirements shall be satisfied: (a) The witnesses shall be adults. (b) The attorney-in-fact may not act as a witness. (c) Each witness signing the power of attorney shall witness either the signing of the instrument by the principal or the principal's acknowledgment of the signature or the power of attorney."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4122 (California Legislative Information text), witness qualifications (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4122)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a power of attorney's execution formalities work under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs the execution of a specific power of attorney. Formality requirements (notary vs. witnesses, witness qualifications) vary by state.

DURABILITY — SURVIVING THE PRINCIPAL'S INCAPACITY
A power of attorney is not automatically revoked by Jordan Alex Lee's later incapacity if the document itself says so — either by stating that it "shall not be affected by subsequent incapacity of the principal," or by similar words showing that intent. Acts an agent takes under a durable power of attorney during a period of the principal's incapacity have the same legal effect, and bind Jordan Alex Lee and Jordan Alex Lee's successors in interest, as if Jordan Alex Lee had full capacity at the time.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A durable power of attorney is a power of attorney by which a principal designates another person as attorney-in-fact in writing and the power of attorney contains any of the following statements: (a) "This power of attorney shall not be affected by subsequent incapacity of the principal." ... (c) Similar words showing the intent of the principal that the authority conferred shall be exercisable notwithstanding the principal's subsequent incapacity."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4124 (California Legislative Information text), durability requires specific language in the document (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4124)
  "All acts done by an attorney-in-fact pursuant to a durable power of attorney during any period of incapacity of the principal have the same effect and inure to the benefit of and bind the principal and the principal's successors in interest as if the principal had capacity."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4125 (California Legislative Information text), acts during incapacity bind the principal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4125)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how durability provisions function under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. Whether a power of attorney is durable by default, or only by express language, differs by state.

IMMEDIATE VS. SPRINGING EFFECTIVENESS
A power of attorney's document can state that it becomes effective immediately upon signing, or instead state that it becomes effective only upon a later event — most commonly, Jordan Alex Lee's incapacity ("springing"). Where a springing structure is used, Jordan Alex Lee can designate one or more persons who determine, by a written declaration signed under penalty of perjury, that the triggering event or contingency (such as incapacity) has occurred; that designated person can be Morgan Lee, someone else, or several people acting jointly. Once that written declaration is executed, the power of attorney becomes effective, and a person may rely on it without liability, regardless of whether the specified event actually occurred.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  ""This power of attorney shall become effective upon the incapacity of the principal.""
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4124(b) (California Legislative Information text), statutory language for a springing (incapacity-triggered) power of attorney (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4124)
  "In a springing power of attorney, the principal may designate one or more persons who, by a written declaration under penalty of perjury, have the power to determine conclusively that the specified event or contingency has occurred. The principal may designate the attorney-in-fact or another person to perform this function, either alone or jointly with other persons. (b) A springing power of attorney containing the designation described in subdivision (a) becomes effective when the person or persons designated in the power of attorney execute a written declaration under penalty of perjury that the specified event or contingency has occurred, and any person may act in reliance on the written declaration without liability to the principal or to any other person, regardless of whether the specified event or contingency has actually occurred."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4129 (California Legislative Information text), mechanism for determining a springing power of attorney's trigger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4129)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a springing power of attorney's triggering mechanism works under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The named-person determination method described here is one mechanism this state's statute makes available; it states elsewhere that it is not the only way a document may condition its own effectiveness.

WHAT A GENERAL GRANT OF AUTHORITY ACTUALLY COVERS
When a statutory-form power of attorney grants authority over "real property transactions," California law construes that grant to empower the agent to buy, sell, lease, mortgage, exchange, manage, insure, and otherwise deal with an interest in real property or a right incident to it, including paying or contesting taxes and assessments and making repairs or alterations — unless the document itself limits or extends that authority. Similarly, a grant of authority over "banking and other financial institution transactions" empowers the agent to open, modify, and close accounts, use a safe deposit box, withdraw funds, endorse and negotiate checks and notes, borrow money and pledge personal property as security, and apply for letters of credit or credit cards, among other listed banking acts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "In a statutory form power of attorney, the language granting power with respect to real property transactions empowers the agent to do all of the following: (a) Accept as a gift or as security for a loan, reject, demand, buy, lease, receive, or otherwise acquire, an interest in real property or a right incident to real property. (b) Sell, exchange, convey with or without covenants, quitclaim, release, surrender, mortgage, encumber, partition, consent to partitioning, subdivide, apply for zoning, rezoning, or other governmental permits, plat or consent to platting, develop, grant options concerning, lease, sublease, or otherwise dispose of, an interest in real property or a right incident to real property. ... (d) Do any act of management or of conservation with respect to an interest in real property, or a right incident to real property, owned, or claimed to be owned, by the principal, including all of the following: (1) Insuring against a casualty, liability, or loss. (2) Obtaining or regaining possession, or protecting the interest or right, by litigation or otherwise. (3) Paying, compromising, or contesting taxes or assessments, or applying for and receiving refunds in connection with them. (4) Purchasing supplies, hiring assistance or labor, and making repairs or alterations in the real property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4451(a)-(b), (d) (California Legislative Information text), scope of authority over real property transactions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4451)
  "In a statutory form power of attorney, the language granting power with respect to banking and other financial institution transactions empowers the agent to do all of the following: (a) Continue, modify, and terminate an account or other banking arrangement made by or on behalf of the principal. (b) Establish, modify, and terminate an account or other banking arrangement with a bank, trust company, savings and loan association, credit union, thrift company, industrial loan company, brokerage firm, or other financial institution selected by the agent. (c) Hire or close a safe deposit box or space in a vault. ... (e) Withdraw by check, order, or otherwise money or property of the principal deposited with or left in the custody of a financial institution. ... (h) Borrow money at an interest rate agreeable to the agent and pledge as security personal property of the principal necessary in order to borrow, pay, renew, or extend the time of payment of a debt of the principal. (i) Make, assign, draw, endorse, discount, guarantee, and negotiate promissory notes, checks, drafts, and other negotiable or nonnegotiable paper of the principal, or payable to the principal or the principal's order, receive the cash or other proceeds of those transactions, and accept a draft drawn by a person upon the principal and pay it when due. ... (k) Apply for and receive letters of credit, credit cards, and traveler's checks from a financial institution, and give an indemnity or other agreement in connection with letters of credit."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4455(a)-(c), (e), (h), (i), (k) (California Legislative Information text), scope of authority over banking transactions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4455)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a general grant of authority over a named subject (like real property or banking) is actually construed under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs the interpretation of a specific power of attorney. This construction specifically applies to the statutory-form power of attorney under this state's law; a custom-drafted document's language could be construed differently.

POWERS THAT REQUIRE EXPRESS, SPECIFIC AUTHORIZATION
Even under a broad general grant of authority, an agent may perform certain acts only if the power of attorney expressly grants that specific authority. That defined list includes: creating, modifying, revoking, or terminating a trust; funding a trust the principal didn't create; making or revoking a gift of the principal's property; disclaiming or renouncing an interest in an estate, trust, or other fund; creating or changing survivorship interests in the principal's property; designating or changing a beneficiary designation on property, a benefit, or a contract right payable on the principal's death; and making a loan to the agent. Separately, no power of attorney — even with express, specific language — may authorize an agent to make, publish, declare, amend, or revoke Jordan Alex Lee's will.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An attorney-in-fact under a power of attorney may perform any of the following acts on behalf of the principal or with the property of the principal only if the power of attorney expressly grants that authority to the attorney-in-fact: (a) Create, modify, revoke, or terminate a trust, in whole or in part ... (c) Make or revoke a gift of the principal's property in trust or otherwise. (d) Exercise the right to reject, disclaim, release, or consent to a reduction in, or modification of, a share in, or payment from, an estate, trust, or other fund on behalf of the principal ... (e) Create or change survivorship interests in the principal's property or in property in which the principal may have an interest. (f) Designate or change the designation of beneficiaries to receive any property, benefit, or contract right on the principal's death. (g) Make a loan to the attorney-in-fact."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4264 (California Legislative Information text), list of acts requiring express authorization in the document (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4264)
  "A power of attorney may not authorize an attorney-in-fact to make, publish, declare, amend, or revoke the principal's will."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4265 (California Legislative Information text), categorical prohibition on will-making authority, regardless of express authorization (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4265)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a defined category of powers requires express, specific authorization in the document — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney, and not a claim that this exact list matches every state's list of powers requiring express authorization.

THE AGENT'S CORE FIDUCIARY DUTIES
An agent acting under a power of attorney has a duty to act solely in Jordan Alex Lee's interest and to avoid conflicts of interest; an agent does not violate that duty solely by also personally benefiting from acting for Jordan Alex Lee, or by having some conflicting interest in the property, care, or affairs involved. Separately, an agent has a duty to keep records of every transaction entered into on Jordan Alex Lee's behalf, though the duty to render an accounting of those records arises only in specific circumstances — such as when Jordan Alex Lee requests it, the document itself requires it, a court orders it, or (after Jordan Alex Lee's death) the request comes from Jordan Alex Lee's personal representative or successor in interest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An attorney-in-fact has a duty to act solely in the interest of the principal and to avoid conflicts of interest. (b) An attorney-in-fact is not in violation of the duty provided in subdivision (a) solely because the attorney-in-fact also benefits from acting for the principal, has conflicting interests in relation to the property, care, or affairs of the principal, or acts in an inconsistent manner regarding the respective interests of the principal and the attorney-in-fact."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4232 (California Legislative Information text), duty of loyalty / avoiding conflicts of interest (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4232)
  "The attorney-in-fact shall keep records of all transactions entered into by the attorney-in-fact on behalf of the principal. (b) The attorney-in-fact does not have a duty to make an account of transactions entered into on behalf of the principal, except in the following circumstances: (1) At any time requested by the principal. (2) Where the power of attorney requires the attorney-in-fact to account and specifies to whom the account is to be made. (3) On request by the conservator of the estate of the principal while the principal is living. (4) On request by the principal's personal representative or successor in interest after the death of the principal. (5) Pursuant to court order."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4236 (California Legislative Information text), duty to keep records; when an accounting is required (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4236)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the fiduciary duties an agent owes under a power of attorney under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The precise content and triggers of these duties vary by state.

THE STANDARD OF CARE AN AGENT IS HELD TO
In dealing with Jordan Alex Lee's property, an agent must observe the standard of care a prudent person would observe in dealing with someone else's property — a standard that is not limited by other statutes that otherwise restrict fiduciary investments. If Morgan Lee has, or was selected based on representations of, special skills or expertise, Morgan Lee is held to the higher standard of care that others with that same skill or expertise would observe. Where Jordan Alex Lee names co-agents, one agent is not liable for another co-agent's actions unless that agent participates in, knowingly acquiesces in, or conceals the other agent's breach of fiduciary duty.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b), in dealing with property of the principal, an attorney-in-fact shall observe the standard of care that would be observed by a prudent person dealing with property of another and is not limited by any other statute restricting investments by fiduciaries. (b) An attorney-in-fact who has special skills or expertise or was designated as an attorney-in-fact on the basis of representations of special skills or expertise shall observe the standard of care that would be observed by others with similar skills or expertise."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4231 (California Legislative Information text), prudent-person standard of care; heightened standard for special skill/expertise (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4231)
  "An attorney-in-fact is not liable for the actions of other attorneys-in-fact, unless the attorney-in-fact participates in, knowingly acquiesces in, or conceals a breach of fiduciary duty committed by another attorney-in-fact."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4202(e) (California Legislative Information text), no vicarious liability among co-agents absent participation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4202)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the standard of care an agent under a power of attorney is held to under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The applicable standard, and any heightened-skill exception, vary by state.

CO-AGENTS AND SUCCESSOR AGENTS
Jordan Alex Lee may designate more than one agent. Absent contrary instructions in the document, authority granted to two or more agents is exercisable only by their unanimous action — but if one agent is unavailable due to absence, illness, or other temporary incapacity, or if a vacancy occurs, the remaining agent(s) may act alone where necessary to accomplish the document's purpose or avoid irreparable injury to Jordan Alex Lee's interests. Jordan Alex Lee may also designate one or more successor agents — such as Casey Lee — to act if a prior agent's authority terminates; a successor agent is not liable for a predecessor's actions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A principal may designate more than one attorney-in-fact in one or more powers of attorney. (b) Authority granted to two or more attorneys-in-fact is exercisable only by their unanimous action. (c) If a vacancy occurs, the remaining attorneys-in-fact may exercise the authority conferred as if they are the only attorneys-in-fact. (d) If an attorney-in-fact is unavailable because of absence, illness, or other temporary incapacity, the other attorneys-in-fact may exercise the authority under the power of attorney as if they are the only attorneys-in-fact, where necessary to accomplish the purposes of the power of attorney or to avoid irreparable injury to the principal's interests."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4202 (California Legislative Information text), default unanimity rule for co-agents, and exceptions for vacancy/unavailability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4202)
  "A principal may designate one or more successor attorneys-in-fact to act if the authority of a predecessor attorney-in-fact terminates. (b) The principal may grant authority to another person, designated by name, by office, or by function, including the initial and any successor attorneys-in-fact, to designate at any time one or more successor attorneys-in-fact. (c) A successor attorney-in-fact is not liable for the actions of the predecessor attorney-in-fact."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4203 (California Legislative Information text), successor agents; no liability for a predecessor's acts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4203)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the default rule for co-agents and successor agents under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The unanimity default is a background rule the document can override.

A THIRD PARTY'S DUTY TO ACCEPT — AND LIABILITY FOR WRONGFUL REFUSAL
A third party (such as a bank or title company) must accord an agent acting under a power of attorney the same rights and privileges the third party would accord Jordan Alex Lee personally — though the third party is not required to honor the agent's authority or conduct business with the agent in circumstances where Jordan Alex Lee personally could not require the third party to act. If an agent furnishes an affidavit stating that, at the time the agent exercised the power, the agent had no actual knowledge that the power of attorney or the agent's authority had been terminated, revoked, or ended by Jordan Alex Lee's death or incapacity, and a third party then refuses to accept the agent's exercise of authority referenced in that affidavit, the third party becomes liable for attorney's fees incurred in any proceeding needed to confirm the agent's authority — unless a court finds the third party believed in good faith that the agent was unqualified or was exceeding or misusing the granted authority.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A third person shall accord an attorney-in-fact acting pursuant to the provisions of a power of attorney the same rights and privileges that would be accorded the principal if the principal were personally present and seeking to act. However, a third person is not required to honor the attorney-in-fact's authority or conduct business with the attorney-in-fact if the principal cannot require the third person to act or conduct business in the same circumstances."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4300 (California Legislative Information text), third party's duty to treat the agent as it would treat the principal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4300)
  "As to acts undertaken in good faith reliance thereon, an affidavit executed by the attorney-in-fact under a power of attorney, whether durable or nondurable, stating that, at the time of the exercise of the power, the attorney-in-fact did not have actual knowledge of the termination of the power of attorney or the attorney-in-fact's authority by revocation or of the principal's death or incapacity is conclusive proof of the nonrevocation or nontermination of the power at that time."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4305(a) (California Legislative Information text), the affidavit's actual required content (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4305.)
  "If an attorney-in-fact furnishes an affidavit pursuant to Section 4305, whether voluntarily or on demand, a third person dealing with the attorney-in-fact who refuses to accept the exercise of the attorney-in-fact's authority referred to in the affidavit is liable for attorney's fees incurred in an action or proceeding necessary to confirm the attorney-in-fact's qualifications or authority, unless the court determines that the third person believed in good faith that the attorney-in-fact was not qualified or was attempting to exceed or improperly exercise the attorney-in-fact's authority."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4306(a) (California Legislative Information text), attorney's-fee liability for refusing to accept an agent's authority after an affidavit is furnished, and its good-faith exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4306)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a third party's duty to accept a power of attorney and a mechanism imposing liability for wrongful refusal under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The fee-liability mechanism described here is specifically tied to a statutory affidavit procedure and its good-faith exception, not a general damages remedy for any refusal.

HOW AND WHEN A POWER OF ATTORNEY IS REVOKED
Jordan Alex Lee may revoke a power of attorney in accordance with any revocation procedure the document itself specifies, or simply by a writing — the writing method is available regardless of what the document says, and cannot be limited or taken away by the document's own terms. Separately, if Jordan Alex Lee grants inconsistent authority to one or more agents across two or more powers of attorney, the authority granted in the later document controls to the extent the two are inconsistent; this rule, too, cannot be limited by the document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A principal may revoke a power of attorney as follows: (1) In accordance with the terms of the power of attorney. (2) By a writing. This paragraph is not subject to limitation in the power of attorney."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4151 (California Legislative Information text), revocation while the principal has capacity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4151)
  "If a principal grants inconsistent authority to one or more attorneys-in-fact in two or more powers of attorney, the authority granted last controls to the extent of the inconsistency. (b) This section is not subject to limitation in the power of attorney."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4130 (California Legislative Information text), later power of attorney controls to the extent of inconsistency (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4130)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how revocation and later-document conflicts work under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney.

WHAT ENDS THE POWER OF ATTORNEY OR AN AGENT'S AUTHORITY
An agent's authority under a power of attorney terminates on any of several statutory events, including: fulfillment or extinction of the document's purpose; revocation; Jordan Alex Lee's death (except as to specific authority a statute permits to be exercised after death); removal or resignation of the agent; the agent's incapacity (a temporary incapacity only suspends authority during the incapacity itself); dissolution or annulment of a marriage between Jordan Alex Lee and a spouse-agent; and the agent's death. This entire list of terminating events carries a general protection: an agent or third party who acts in good faith without notice that any one of these events has occurred is protected from liability for that action — not only in the specific case of Jordan Alex Lee's death, which a separate statute states explicitly.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Subject to subdivision (b), the authority of an attorney-in-fact under a power of attorney is terminated by any of the following events: (1) In accordance with the terms of the power of attorney. (2) Extinction of the subject or fulfillment of the purpose of the power of attorney. (3) Revocation of the attorney-in-fact's authority, as provided in Section 4153. (4) Death of the principal, except as to specific authority permitted by statute to be exercised after the principal's death. (5) Removal of the attorney-in-fact. (6) Resignation of the attorney-in-fact. (7) Incapacity of the attorney-in-fact, except that a temporary incapacity suspends the attorney-in-fact's authority only during the period of the incapacity. (8) Dissolution or annulment of the marriage of the attorney-in-fact and principal, as provided in Section 4154. (9) Death of the attorney-in-fact. (b) An attorney-in-fact or third person who does not have notice of an event that terminates the power of attorney or the authority of an attorney-in-fact is protected from liability as provided in Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 4300)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4152 (California Legislative Information text), statutory list of events terminating an agent's authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4152)
  "The death of a principal who has executed a power of attorney, whether durable or nondurable, does not revoke or terminate the agency as to the attorney-in-fact or a third person who, without actual knowledge of the principal's death, acts in good faith under the power of attorney. Any action so taken, unless otherwise invalid or unenforceable, binds the principal's successors in interest."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4304(a) (California Legislative Information text), good-faith acts without knowledge of the principal's death remain binding (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4304)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what events terminate a power of attorney or an agent's authority under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney.

SIGNATURE, WITNESS, AND NOTARIZATION
Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

Two-witness option (used only if this document is not notarized):
Witness 1 — Signature: ☐ _________________________ Printed name: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________
Witness 2 — Signature: ☐ _________________________ Printed name: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

Notary acknowledgment option (used only if this document is not witnessed):
State of ☐ _________________________, County of ☐ _________________________
On ☐ _________________________, before me, personally appeared Jordan Alex Lee, proved to me on the basis of satisfactory evidence to be the person whose name is subscribed to this instrument.
Notary signature: ☐ _________________________ Printed name: ☐ _________________________ Commission expires: ☐ _________________________

citations.quote: A durable power of attorney is a power of attorney by which a principal designates another person as attorney-in-fact in writing and the power of attorney contains any of the following statements: (a) "This power of attorney shall not be affected by subsequent incapacity of the principal." ... (c) Similar words showing the intent of the principal that the authority conferred shall be exercisable notwithstanding the principal's subsequent incapacity.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4125 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: acts during incapacity bind the principal
citations.quote: All acts done by an attorney-in-fact pursuant to a durable power of attorney during any period of incapacity of the principal have the same effect and inure to the benefit of and bind the principal and the principal's successors in interest as if the principal had capacity.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how durability provisions function under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. Whether a power of attorney is durable by default, or only by express language, differs by state.

expectedJSON.body: A power of attorney's document can state that it becomes effective immediately upon signing, or instead state that it becomes effective only upon a later event — most commonly, Jordan Alex Lee's incapacity ("springing"). Where a springing structure is used, Jordan Alex Lee can designate one or more persons who determine, by a written declaration signed under penalty of perjury, that the triggering event or contingency (such as incapacity) has occurred; that designated person can be Morgan Lee, someone else, or several people acting jointly. Once that written declaration is executed, the power of attorney becomes effective, and a person may rely on it without liability, regardless of whether the specified event actually occurred.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4124(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: statutory language for a springing (incapacity-triggered) power of attorney
citations.quote: "This power of attorney shall become effective upon the incapacity of the principal."

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4129 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: mechanism for determining a springing power of attorney's trigger
citations.quote: In a springing power of attorney, the principal may designate one or more persons who, by a written declaration under penalty of perjury, have the power to determine conclusively that the specified event or contingency has occurred. The principal may designate the attorney-in-fact or another person to perform this function, either alone or jointly with other persons. (b) A springing power of attorney containing the designation described in subdivision (a) becomes effective when the person or persons designated in the power of attorney execute a written declaration under penalty of perjury that the specified event or contingency has occurred, and any person may act in reliance on the written declaration without liability to the principal or to any other person, regardless of whether the specified event or contingency has actually occurred.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a springing power of attorney's triggering mechanism works under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The named-person determination method described here is one mechanism this state's statute makes available; it states elsewhere that it is not the only way a document may condition its own effectiveness.

expectedJSON.body: When a statutory-form power of attorney grants authority over "real property transactions," California law construes that grant to empower the agent to buy, sell, lease, mortgage, exchange, manage, insure, and otherwise deal with an interest in real property or a right incident to it, including paying or contesting taxes and assessments and making repairs or alterations — unless the document itself limits or extends that authority. Similarly, a grant of authority over "banking and other financial institution transactions" empowers the agent to open, modify, and close accounts, use a safe deposit box, withdraw funds, endorse and negotiate checks and notes, borrow money and pledge personal property as security, and apply for letters of credit or credit cards, among other listed banking acts.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4451(a)-(b), (d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: scope of authority over real property transactions
citations.quote: In a statutory form power of attorney, the language granting power with respect to real property transactions empowers the agent to do all of the following: (a) Accept as a gift or as security for a loan, reject, demand, buy, lease, receive, or otherwise acquire, an interest in real property or a right incident to real property. (b) Sell, exchange, convey with or without covenants, quitclaim, release, surrender, mortgage, encumber, partition, consent to partitioning, subdivide, apply for zoning, rezoning, or other governmental permits, plat or consent to platting, develop, grant options concerning, lease, sublease, or otherwise dispose of, an interest in real property or a right incident to real property. ... (d) Do any act of management or of conservation with respect to an interest in real property, or a right incident to real property, owned, or claimed to be owned, by the principal, including all of the following: (1) Insuring against a casualty, liability, or loss. (2) Obtaining or regaining possession, or protecting the interest or right, by litigation or otherwise. (3) Paying, compromising, or contesting taxes or assessments, or applying for and receiving refunds in connection with them. (4) Purchasing supplies, hiring assistance or labor, and making repairs or alterations in the real property.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4455(a)-(c), (e), (h), (i), (k) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: scope of authority over banking transactions
citations.quote: In a statutory form power of attorney, the language granting power with respect to banking and other financial institution transactions empowers the agent to do all of the following: (a) Continue, modify, and terminate an account or other banking arrangement made by or on behalf of the principal. (b) Establish, modify, and terminate an account or other banking arrangement with a bank, trust company, savings and loan association, credit union, thrift company, industrial loan company, brokerage firm, or other financial institution selected by the agent. (c) Hire or close a safe deposit box or space in a vault. ... (e) Withdraw by check, order, or otherwise money or property of the principal deposited with or left in the custody of a financial institution. ... (h) Borrow money at an interest rate agreeable to the agent and pledge as security personal property of the principal necessary in order to borrow, pay, renew, or extend the time of payment of a debt of the principal. (i) Make, assign, draw, endorse, discount, guarantee, and negotiate promissory notes, checks, drafts, and other negotiable or nonnegotiable paper of the principal, or payable to the principal or the principal's order, receive the cash or other proceeds of those transactions, and accept a draft drawn by a person upon the principal and pay it when due. ... (k) Apply for and receive letters of credit, credit cards, and traveler's checks from a financial institution, and give an indemnity or other agreement in connection with letters of credit.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a general grant of authority over a named subject (like real property or banking) is actually construed under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs the interpretation of a specific power of attorney. This construction specifically applies to the statutory-form power of attorney under this state's law; a custom-drafted document's language could be construed differently.

expectedJSON.body: Even under a broad general grant of authority, an agent may perform certain acts only if the power of attorney expressly grants that specific authority. That defined list includes: creating, modifying, revoking, or terminating a trust; funding a trust the principal didn't create; making or revoking a gift of the principal's property; disclaiming or renouncing an interest in an estate, trust, or other fund; creating or changing survivorship interests in the principal's property; designating or changing a beneficiary designation on property, a benefit, or a contract right payable on the principal's death; and making a loan to the agent. Separately, no power of attorney — even with express, specific language — may authorize an agent to make, publish, declare, amend, or revoke Jordan Alex Lee's will.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4264 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: list of acts requiring express authorization in the document
citations.quote: An attorney-in-fact under a power of attorney may perform any of the following acts on behalf of the principal or with the property of the principal only if the power of attorney expressly grants that authority to the attorney-in-fact: (a) Create, modify, revoke, or terminate a trust, in whole or in part ... (c) Make or revoke a gift of the principal's property in trust or otherwise. (d) Exercise the right to reject, disclaim, release, or consent to a reduction in, or modification of, a share in, or payment from, an estate, trust, or other fund on behalf of the principal ... (e) Create or change survivorship interests in the principal's property or in property in which the principal may have an interest. (f) Designate or change the designation of beneficiaries to receive any property, benefit, or contract right on the principal's death. (g) Make a loan to the attorney-in-fact.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4265 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: categorical prohibition on will-making authority, regardless of express authorization
citations.quote: A power of attorney may not authorize an attorney-in-fact to make, publish, declare, amend, or revoke the principal's will.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a defined category of powers requires express, specific authorization in the document — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney, and not a claim that this exact list matches every state's list of powers requiring express authorization.

expectedJSON.body: An agent acting under a power of attorney has a duty to act solely in Jordan Alex Lee's interest and to avoid conflicts of interest; an agent does not violate that duty solely by also personally benefiting from acting for Jordan Alex Lee, or by having some conflicting interest in the property, care, or affairs involved. Separately, an agent has a duty to keep records of every transaction entered into on Jordan Alex Lee's behalf, though the duty to render an accounting of those records arises only in specific circumstances — such as when Jordan Alex Lee requests it, the document itself requires it, a court orders it, or (after Jordan Alex Lee's death) the request comes from Jordan Alex Lee's personal representative or successor in interest.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4232 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: duty of loyalty / avoiding conflicts of interest
citations.quote: An attorney-in-fact has a duty to act solely in the interest of the principal and to avoid conflicts of interest. (b) An attorney-in-fact is not in violation of the duty provided in subdivision (a) solely because the attorney-in-fact also benefits from acting for the principal, has conflicting interests in relation to the property, care, or affairs of the principal, or acts in an inconsistent manner regarding the respective interests of the principal and the attorney-in-fact.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4236 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: duty to keep records; when an accounting is required
citations.quote: The attorney-in-fact shall keep records of all transactions entered into by the attorney-in-fact on behalf of the principal. (b) The attorney-in-fact does not have a duty to make an account of transactions entered into on behalf of the principal, except in the following circumstances: (1) At any time requested by the principal. (2) Where the power of attorney requires the attorney-in-fact to account and specifies to whom the account is to be made. (3) On request by the conservator of the estate of the principal while the principal is living. (4) On request by the principal's personal representative or successor in interest after the death of the principal. (5) Pursuant to court order.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the fiduciary duties an agent owes under a power of attorney under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The precise content and triggers of these duties vary by state.

expectedJSON.body: In dealing with Jordan Alex Lee's property, an agent must observe the standard of care a prudent person would observe in dealing with someone else's property — a standard that is not limited by other statutes that otherwise restrict fiduciary investments. If Morgan Lee has, or was selected based on representations of, special skills or expertise, Morgan Lee is held to the higher standard of care that others with that same skill or expertise would observe. Where Jordan Alex Lee names co-agents, one agent is not liable for another co-agent's actions unless that agent participates in, knowingly acquiesces in, or conceals the other agent's breach of fiduciary duty.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4231 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: prudent-person standard of care; heightened standard for special skill/expertise
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), in dealing with property of the principal, an attorney-in-fact shall observe the standard of care that would be observed by a prudent person dealing with property of another and is not limited by any other statute restricting investments by fiduciaries. (b) An attorney-in-fact who has special skills or expertise or was designated as an attorney-in-fact on the basis of representations of special skills or expertise shall observe the standard of care that would be observed by others with similar skills or expertise.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4202(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no vicarious liability among co-agents absent participation
citations.quote: An attorney-in-fact is not liable for the actions of other attorneys-in-fact, unless the attorney-in-fact participates in, knowingly acquiesces in, or conceals a breach of fiduciary duty committed by another attorney-in-fact.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the standard of care an agent under a power of attorney is held to under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The applicable standard, and any heightened-skill exception, vary by state.

expectedJSON.body: Jordan Alex Lee may designate more than one agent. Absent contrary instructions in the document, authority granted to two or more agents is exercisable only by their unanimous action — but if one agent is unavailable due to absence, illness, or other temporary incapacity, or if a vacancy occurs, the remaining agent(s) may act alone where necessary to accomplish the document's purpose or avoid irreparable injury to Jordan Alex Lee's interests. Jordan Alex Lee may also designate one or more successor agents — such as Casey Lee — to act if a prior agent's authority terminates; a successor agent is not liable for a predecessor's actions.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4202 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: default unanimity rule for co-agents, and exceptions for vacancy/unavailability
citations.quote: A principal may designate more than one attorney-in-fact in one or more powers of attorney. (b) Authority granted to two or more attorneys-in-fact is exercisable only by their unanimous action. (c) If a vacancy occurs, the remaining attorneys-in-fact may exercise the authority conferred as if they are the only attorneys-in-fact. (d) If an attorney-in-fact is unavailable because of absence, illness, or other temporary incapacity, the other attorneys-in-fact may exercise the authority under the power of attorney as if they are the only attorneys-in-fact, where necessary to accomplish the purposes of the power of attorney or to avoid irreparable injury to the principal's interests.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4203 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: successor agents; no liability for a predecessor's acts
citations.quote: A principal may designate one or more successor attorneys-in-fact to act if the authority of a predecessor attorney-in-fact terminates. (b) The principal may grant authority to another person, designated by name, by office, or by function, including the initial and any successor attorneys-in-fact, to designate at any time one or more successor attorneys-in-fact. (c) A successor attorney-in-fact is not liable for the actions of the predecessor attorney-in-fact.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the default rule for co-agents and successor agents under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The unanimity default is a background rule the document can override.

expectedJSON.body: A third party (such as a bank or title company) must accord an agent acting under a power of attorney the same rights and privileges the third party would accord Jordan Alex Lee personally — though the third party is not required to honor the agent's authority or conduct business with the agent in circumstances where Jordan Alex Lee personally could not require the third party to act. If an agent furnishes an affidavit stating that, at the time the agent exercised the power, the agent had no actual knowledge that the power of attorney or the agent's authority had been terminated, revoked, or ended by Jordan Alex Lee's death or incapacity, and a third party then refuses to accept the agent's exercise of authority referenced in that affidavit, the third party becomes liable for attorney's fees incurred in any proceeding needed to confirm the agent's authority — unless a court finds the third party believed in good faith that the agent was unqualified or was exceeding or misusing the granted authority.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4300 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: third party's duty to treat the agent as it would treat the principal
citations.quote: A third person shall accord an attorney-in-fact acting pursuant to the provisions of a power of attorney the same rights and privileges that would be accorded the principal if the principal were personally present and seeking to act. However, a third person is not required to honor the attorney-in-fact's authority or conduct business with the attorney-in-fact if the principal cannot require the third person to act or conduct business in the same circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4305(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the affidavit's actual required content
citations.quote: As to acts undertaken in good faith reliance thereon, an affidavit executed by the attorney-in-fact under a power of attorney, whether durable or nondurable, stating that, at the time of the exercise of the power, the attorney-in-fact did not have actual knowledge of the termination of the power of attorney or the attorney-in-fact's authority by revocation or of the principal's death or incapacity is conclusive proof of the nonrevocation or nontermination of the power at that time.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4306(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: attorney's-fee liability for refusing to accept an agent's authority after an affidavit is furnished, and its good-faith exception
citations.quote: If an attorney-in-fact furnishes an affidavit pursuant to Section 4305, whether voluntarily or on demand, a third person dealing with the attorney-in-fact who refuses to accept the exercise of the attorney-in-fact's authority referred to in the affidavit is liable for attorney's fees incurred in an action or proceeding necessary to confirm the attorney-in-fact's qualifications or authority, unless the court determines that the third person believed in good faith that the attorney-in-fact was not qualified or was attempting to exceed or improperly exercise the attorney-in-fact's authority.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a third party's duty to accept a power of attorney and a mechanism imposing liability for wrongful refusal under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The fee-liability mechanism described here is specifically tied to a statutory affidavit procedure and its good-faith exception, not a general damages remedy for any refusal.

expectedJSON.body: Jordan Alex Lee may revoke a power of attorney in accordance with any revocation procedure the document itself specifies, or simply by a writing — the writing method is available regardless of what the document says, and cannot be limited or taken away by the document's own terms. Separately, if Jordan Alex Lee grants inconsistent authority to one or more agents across two or more powers of attorney, the authority granted in the later document controls to the extent the two are inconsistent; this rule, too, cannot be limited by the document.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4151 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: revocation while the principal has capacity
citations.quote: A principal may revoke a power of attorney as follows: (1) In accordance with the terms of the power of attorney. (2) By a writing. This paragraph is not subject to limitation in the power of attorney.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4130 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: later power of attorney controls to the extent of inconsistency
citations.quote: If a principal grants inconsistent authority to one or more attorneys-in-fact in two or more powers of attorney, the authority granted last controls to the extent of the inconsistency. (b) This section is not subject to limitation in the power of attorney.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how revocation and later-document conflicts work under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney.

expectedJSON.body: An agent's authority under a power of attorney terminates on any of several statutory events, including: fulfillment or extinction of the document's purpose; revocation; Jordan Alex Lee's death (except as to specific authority a statute permits to be exercised after death); removal or resignation of the agent; the agent's incapacity (a temporary incapacity only suspends authority during the incapacity itself); dissolution or annulment of a marriage between Jordan Alex Lee and a spouse-agent; and the agent's death. This entire list of terminating events carries a general protection: an agent or third party who acts in good faith without notice that any one of these events has occurred is protected from liability for that action — not only in the specific case of Jordan Alex Lee's death, which a separate statute states explicitly.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4152 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: statutory list of events terminating an agent's authority
citations.quote: (a) Subject to subdivision (b), the authority of an attorney-in-fact under a power of attorney is terminated by any of the following events: (1) In accordance with the terms of the power of attorney. (2) Extinction of the subject or fulfillment of the purpose of the power of attorney. (3) Revocation of the attorney-in-fact's authority, as provided in Section 4153. (4) Death of the principal, except as to specific authority permitted by statute to be exercised after the principal's death. (5) Removal of the attorney-in-fact. (6) Resignation of the attorney-in-fact. (7) Incapacity of the attorney-in-fact, except that a temporary incapacity suspends the attorney-in-fact's authority only during the period of the incapacity. (8) Dissolution or annulment of the marriage of the attorney-in-fact and principal, as provided in Section 4154. (9) Death of the attorney-in-fact. (b) An attorney-in-fact or third person who does not have notice of an event that terminates the power of attorney or the authority of an attorney-in-fact is protected from liability as provided in Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 4300).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4304(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: good-faith acts without knowledge of the principal's death remain binding
citations.quote: The death of a principal who has executed a power of attorney, whether durable or nondurable, does not revoke or terminate the agency as to the attorney-in-fact or a third person who, without actual knowledge of the principal's death, acts in good faith under the power of attorney. Any action so taken, unless otherwise invalid or unenforceable, binds the principal's successors in interest.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what events terminate a power of attorney or an agent's authority under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney.
